identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Grishneshwar is counted among the twelve Jyotirlingas of Shiva, and is widely treated as the last of the twelve. It stands in Verul village about a kilometre and a half from the Ellora Caves, so the living Jyotirlinga sits beside one of the great rock-cut complexes of the Deccan. The temple takes its name from the devotee Ghushma of its sthala-purana, whose son Shiva is said to have restored to her at this spot.

governance.establishedEra: Rebuilt in its present form in the 18th century, on a site restored in the 16th century by Maloji Bhosale after earlier destruction
governance.founderPatron: 16th-century restoration attributed to Maloji Bhosale; the 18th-century rebuilding attributed by Wikipedia to Gautama Bai Holkar of Indore in 1729, and elsewhere to Ahilyabai Holkar — see narrative notes

narrative.documentedHistory:
Grishneshwar stands in Verul village in the district of Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (formerly Aurangabad), roughly 1.5 km from the Ellora Caves and about 30 km north-west of the district city. Its position beside the Ellora escarpment places a continuously worshipped Shaiva shrine immediately next to one of the largest rock-cut cave complexes in India.

The temple's fabric records a cycle of destruction and rebuilding. An earlier structure was destroyed during the Delhi Sultanate period in the 13th-14th centuries. A restoration in the 16th century is attributed to Maloji Bhosale, grandfather of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, and further damage followed during the Mughal-Maratha conflicts. The present temple is an 18th-century Holkar rebuilding: the Wikipedia article on the temple dates it to 1729 under the sponsorship of Gautama Bai Holkar of Indore, while the attribution most commonly repeated in travel and reference writing is to Ahilyabai Holkar, who is also credited with rebuilding Kashi Vishwanath. No government or trust source confirming either attribution was located, so both are recorded and neither is stated as settled.

Architecturally, the temple is built of stone in the Hemadpanthi idiom of the Deccan and spans an area given as about 44,000 sq ft; its interior and exterior walls carry sculpture and carved ornament. The garbhagriha holds the Jyotirlinga, and a large Nandi stands before the main door. The temple is a nationally protected monument.

A local tradition, described as such rather than as a posted rule, requires men to enter the garbhagriha bare-chested.
narrative.sthalaPuranam: The temple's traditional account concerns Ghushma (also given as Kusuma), a devotee who daily made and worshipped 101 earthen Shiva lingas. Her son was killed by a jealous co-wife and his body thrown into a pond; Shiva, moved by her constancy, restored the boy to her, and the deity is said to have remained at this place as Ghrishneshwar.
narrative.architectureStyle: Hemadpanthi, stone-built, over an area given as about 44,000 sq ft

visitingInfo.entryRules: Local Hindu tradition at this temple requires men to go bare-chested to enter the garbhagriha. Described in reference sources as a customary practice rather than a posted temple regulation; confirm on arrival.
visitingInfo.officialContactNote: No temple trust website or telephone number could be confirmed from a government or trust source. The site that presents itself as the temple's official page names no trust and is run by a third-party portal, so its timings should be confirmed at the temple or with the district administration before travelling. The temple is a protected monument, so ASI conditions may apply to the surrounding fabric.
visitingInfo.notes: The previously recorded distances (Aurangabad railway station 30 km, Aurangabad airport 30 km) could not be confirmed from any page opened and are not restated. Sources opened give the temple as about 30 km north-west of Aurangabad city and about 1.5 km from the Ellora Caves. The postal code differs between sources: this directory holds 431111 while the self-styled official site gives 431102, so no postal code is asserted here.
